note: Original content written by an AI agent from general knowledge. Nothing was copied from a course, book, phrasebook or website. Pointing, transliteration (capitals mark the stressed syllable), register labels and gender forms have NOT been checked by a native speaker. No audio exists for any item. Nothing here was tested with learners.

items.title: The adjective does not match the noun
items.why: Every Hebrew noun is masculine or feminine. A noun ending in -a is usually feminine, and the adjective must match it.
items.fix: When you learn a noun, learn it with its adjective ending: misada tova.

drill.prompt: Pick the correct sentence for 'The restaurant is good'.
drill.explain: Misada is feminine, so the adjective takes -a: tova. Tov is masculine singular; tovim is plural.

items.title: Using the wrong form for your own gender
items.why: Present-tense verbs agree with the speaker: men say rotse, women say rotsa. Learners often use only the masculine form they met first.
items.fix: Practice each phrase in your own form, and in the other form for when you quote someone.
items.say: Say the line three times in your own form.

drill.prompt: Imagine you are a woman. How do you say 'I want water'?
drill.explain: A woman says rotsa. Rotse is the masculine form; rotsim is plural.

items.title: Addressing a woman with a masculine form
items.why: Words like 'you' and the endings -cha / -ech change with the person you speak to.
items.fix: Before you speak, decide who you are talking to. If you are not sure, use a form with no gender, like ma nishma?
items.say: Say: ma shlomcha (to a man), ma shlomech (to a woman).

drill.prompt: You ask a woman how she is. Which is correct?
drill.explain: Shlomech is for a woman, shlomcha for a man, shlomo means 'his well-being'.

items.title: Saying the final 'h' in -eh

wrong.note: with a breath at the end

items.why: A final ה (he) usually only shows the vowel. It is silent. Textbook romanisations like 'rotseh' tempt learners to pronounce an h.
items.fix: Read the last letter as part of the vowel and end the word on the vowel.
items.say: Say: roTSE, roTSA, taleh... end each on the vowel.

drill.prompt: How do people say רוֹצֶה in normal speech?
drill.explain: The final ה marks the vowel and is not pronounced as a consonant.

items.title: Stressing the first syllable
items.why: Most Hebrew words are stressed on the last syllable. English speakers tend to stress the first.
items.fix: Mark the stress in your notes. Practice toDA, bevakaSHA, sliCHA, shaLOM, kaMA.
items.say: Say: toDA, sliCHA, bevakaSHA, with the stress last.

drill.prompt: Which is the usual stress of תּוֹדָה?
drill.explain: Toda is stressed on the last syllable, like most Hebrew words.

items.title: Stressing the last syllable of every word
items.why: Some common nouns, such as boker, layla, sefer, erev, are stressed on the next-to-last syllable. They often have two segol-type vowels.
items.fix: Learn these common words with the stress marked and say them aloud as chunks.

drill.prompt: Which is the usual stress of בֹּקֶר?
drill.explain: Boker is stressed on the first syllable. This is one of the common exceptions to last-syllable stress.

items.title: Saying chet as 'ch' in church or as 'h'
items.why: Chet (ח) and kaf without a dot (כ) are both a rough sound made in the throat, like the ch in Scottish loch. It is not English ch or h.
items.fix: Make an English h, then tighten the back of the throat and add friction.

options.text: a rough sound in the throat, like Scottish 'loch'

drill.explain: Chet is the rough throat sound. Church-ch and plain h are common learner errors.

items.title: Rolling the resh like Spanish or English r
items.why: Many modern Israeli speakers are commonly heard to say resh at the back of the mouth, not with the tip of the tongue. It varies by speaker, so this is a tendency, not a rule.
items.fix: Practise a gentle growl at the back of the mouth, between English r and French r. Do not worry if it is hard: clarity matters more.
items.say: Say: rosh, rega, rakevet, trying the back-of-throat r.

drill.prompt: Which resh is commonly heard in everyday modern Israeli speech?

options.text: an r made at the back of the throat
a rolled r made with the tip of the tongue

drill.explain: A back-of-throat r is commonly heard. Other pronunciations exist: ask a native speaker what they do.

items.confidenceReason: Dialect and generation differences were not checked.

items.title: Saying 'toda raba' for everything
items.why: Plain toda is the commonly heard thanks for small things. Toda raba is warmer and suits a bigger favour. Saying the heavy form for everything can sound over-careful.
items.fix: Use toda for small things, toda raba when someone really helped you.
items.say: Say: toDA, then toDA raBA, with different warmth.

drill.prompt: A stranger holds the door open for you. What is the lightest natural thanks?
drill.explain: Plain toda fits. The other lines are grand for a held door.

items.confidenceReason: Based on general impressions of everyday use, not measured.

items.title: Opening every request with 'I want'
items.why: Ani rotse is understood and not rude, but efshar ...? ('is it possible ...?') is the opener commonly heard when ordering, and it has no gender to get wrong.
items.fix: Start requests with efshar, and add bevakasha.
items.say: Say: efshar kafe? efshar chesbon? efshar lashevet po?

drill.prompt: Which request needs no choice of gender?
drill.explain: Efshar has no gendered word. Rotse/rotsa and ma'adif/ma'adifa change with the speaker.

items.confidenceReason: 'Commonly heard' is a general impression, not measured.

items.title: Saying 'I am have' for 'I have'
items.why: Hebrew has no verb 'to have'. You say 'there is to me': yesh li.
items.fix: Memorise yesh li, yesh lecha, yesh lo as chunks.
items.say: Say: yesh li kesef, yesh li zman.

drill.prompt: How do you say 'I have a sister'?
drill.explain: Yesh li means 'I have'. Ani yesh is a literal English translation.

items.title: Doubling consonants because of a dagesh
items.why: In everyday Israeli Hebrew a dagesh does not usually double the consonant. Reading each pointed vowel and dot as a separate sound can sound like reading a textbook aloud. Likewise kamatz and patach sound the same (a), and tsere and segol sound the same (e).
items.fix: Say each word as one flowing chunk. If a point looks tricky, ask whether it changes the sound in Israeli Hebrew.
items.say: Say: eKACH, hapa'AM, with single consonants.

drill.prompt: How do you say אֶקַּח in normal speech?
drill.explain: A single consonant. The dagesh is a spelling rule, not a doubling in everyday speech.

items.title: Starting every question with 'ha'im'
items.why: Ha'im marks a question in writing and in formal speech. In conversation, a rising voice is enough.
items.fix: Say the statement and lift your voice at the end.
items.say: Say: aTA ba? yesh li? zeh po?

drill.prompt: Which question sounds most natural in a casual chat?
drill.explain: Rising voice alone is natural. The others sound formal or archaic.

items.title: Gliding the vowels like English
items.why: Hebrew has five clean vowels (a, e, i, o, u). English glides (oh-oo, ay-ee) mark an accent right away.
items.fix: Say each vowel and hold your mouth still while you say it.
items.say: Say: a, e, i, o, u; then shaLOM, toDA, ken.

options.text: a clean short o, no glide

drill.explain: A pure o. The glide marks a foreign accent.

items.title: Saying vav as English w
items.why: Vav (ו) as a consonant is v, as in van. Hebrew has no w sound.
items.fix: Put your top teeth on your bottom lip for v.

drill.prompt: How does the first letter of וָואלָה sound?
